record.paper_title: Some Open Problems in Polyomino Tilings
record.original_question: A tiling is k-isohedral if k is the smallest number of classes into which its tiles can be partitioned so that any two tiles in the same class are related by a symmetry of the tiling. A polyomino is k-anisohedral if it has a k-isohedral tiling but has no k'-isohedral tiling for any smaller k'. Does there exist a k-anisohedral polyomino for some k at least 7?

evidence.quote: A tiling T is k-isohedral provided that k is the smallest number of partitions in a partitioning of T such that for any two copies Ti, Tj in a common part, there is a symmetry of T mapping Ti to Tj.
A polyomino is k-anisohedral provided it has a k-isohedral tiling, but not a k′-isohedral tiling for any k′ < k.
Open Problem 6 Does there exist a k-anisohedral polyomino for some k≥ 7?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Work in the Euclidean plane. A polyomino is a finite, edge-connected union of unit squares whose vertices lie on the integer lattice. A tiling of the plane is a covering of the plane by congruent copies of a single polyomino (allowing rotations and reflections) whose interiors are pairwise disjoint. Given a tiling T, a symmetry of T is an isometry of the plane that maps T to itself (sending tiles to tiles). Two tiles of T are said to be equivalent if some symmetry of T sends one to the other; this equivalence partitions the tiles of T into transitivity classes. The tiling T is called k-isohedral if it has exactly k transitivity classes (equivalently, k is the minimum number of parts of a partition of the tiles of T such that any two tiles in the same part are related by a symmetry of T). The isohedral number of a polyomino P is the smallest integer k such that P admits a k-isohedral tiling of the plane (and no k'-isohedral tiling for any k' < k); when this minimum equals k, P is called k-anisohedral.

Question: Does there exist a polyomino whose isohedral number is at least 7? Equivalently, does there exist an integer k ≥ 7 and a polyomino P that admits a k-isohedral tiling of the plane but admits no k'-isohedral tiling for any k' < k?
artifact.status_search_result: For polyominoes specifically, examples of k-anisohedral tiles are known up through k = 6 (results due to Joseph Myers and earlier authors). For polyhexes, Myers has constructed an example with isohedral number 10, and Socolar showed arbitrarily large isohedral numbers are achievable for disconnected or marked tiles. However, no polyomino with isohedral number ≥ 7 has been published, and the question for polyominoes appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Anisohedral tiling - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Joseph Myers has produced a collection of tilings by polyhexes... including a polyhexagon with isohedral number 10.
status_evidence.claim: Largest verified isohedral numbers for polyhex tiles reach 10; no analogous polyomino result is cited.

status_evidence.title: Polyform tiling - polyomino.org.uk
status_evidence.snippet: The anisohedral classification tables for polyominoes list entries through k = 6.
status_evidence.claim: Documented k-anisohedral polyominoes appear only up to k = 6, leaving k ≥ 7 unresolved.
